references.text: The context of the meal where Aaron and his sons are to eat the meat from the ram at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
Describes how the priests and their families are to eat from the offerings in a holy place.
The prohibition against foreigners (non-priests) eating from the holy offerings is further explained here.
The consecration of the priests with anointing and the filling of their hands to set them apart for service.
A parallel account of the priests' consecration and atonement, completed over seven days.
The priests' right to the most holy offerings that belong to them and their sons.
Only male descendants of Aaron among the priests are to eat from the sin offering.
The New Testament refers to an altar from which those who serve in the tabernacle have no right to eat, pointing to Christ as the fulfillment.
All men among the priests may eat from the guilt offering in a holy place, for it is most holy.
Lev 22:10 specifies the definition of 'foreigner' mentioned in Ex 29:33 and clarifies the boundaries of who may eat the holy things.
Lev 10:17 explains the theological reason for the command in Ex 29:33 that priests must eat the sacrificial meat to bear guilt and make atonement.
Lev 6:23 limits the rule in Ex 29:33 by showing that there is a type of sin offering (with blood brought into the sanctuary) that must not be eaten but burned.
Ezek 44:29 confirms and continues the permanent priestly principle from Ex 29:33 that priests are to eat sacrificial meat to make atonement.
Lev 19:8 describes the serious consequence (being cut off) for violating the prohibition against foreigners eating holy things, as commanded in Ex 29:33.
